Single-cell and spatial transcriptome analyses unveil that MYH11 links stemness to immunotherapy resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.

Combining single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, the authors identify a MYH11-high cancer stem cell subpopulation in non-small cell lung cancer that is linked to immunotherapy resistance. The study proposes MYH11 as a marker connecting tumor stemness to immune evasion, suggesting a potential target for overcoming treatment resistance.

Spatial transcriptomics reveals PDIA6 as a tumor-intrinsic driver of mesenchymal plasticity and vascular microenvironment remodeling in glioblastoma.

Using spatial transcriptomics, this study identifies PDIA6 as a tumor-intrinsic driver in glioblastoma that promotes mesenchymal plasticity and remodels the vascular microenvironment, helping create protective perivascular niches. The findings link PDIA6 to malignant-endothelial crosstalk and suggest it contributes to therapy resistance, highlighting it as a potential therapeutic target.

Lineage-mixed neurodevelopmental programs in pediatric sarcomas nominate tumor-selective surface antigen pairs.

The authors analyzed a large single-cell RNA-seq atlas of 266 pediatric solid tumor samples and xenografts, finding that these tumors express mixed lineage neurodevelopmental gene programs reflecting arrested progenitor states. This lineage mixing nominates tumor-selective pairs of surface antigens that could serve as dual-targeting therapeutic vulnerabilities. The work demonstrates how pan-tumor single-cell atlases can reveal shared developmental dependencies across pediatric cancers.

HOMED enables hierarchical and multimodal optimization of DNA methylation deconvolution across tissues.

HOMED is a new computational framework for DNA methylation deconvolution that accounts for hierarchical relationships among related cell types and uses single-cell RNA-seq plus paired bulk RNA-seq/DNAm data to optimize CpG signatures. This improves estimation of cell-type proportions in bulk methylation data across tissues, addressing a key confounder in epigenome-wide association studies.

Categorization and analysis of 16 computational methods for estimating cell potency from single-cell RNA-seq data.

This review categorizes 16 computational methods for estimating cell potency (differentiation potential) from static scRNA-seq data into average-based, entropy-based, and knowledge-based approaches. The authors show these methods rest on different, sometimes conflicting assumptions, and provide a unified mathematical framework for comparing them. The work helps researchers choose appropriate potency-estimation tools and understand their limitations.

CellMarker 3.0: an updated resource of manually curated and computationally predicted cell markers in human/mouse and interactive web tools for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics analysis.

CellMarker 3.0 is an updated database that curates experimentally validated cell-type marker genes for human and mouse tissues, now supplemented with computationally predicted markers. The release adds 274 tissues, 1,877 cell types, 64,040 markers, and over 1.2 million tissue-cell type-marker entries, and introduces interactive web tools for analyzing single-cell RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics data.

A droplet-based long-read single-cell epigenome sequencing method for the high-throughput profiling of multidimensional regulatory elements within individual cells.

The authors developed droplet-based long-read single-cell epigenome sequencing methods, dscNanoATAC and dscNanoCUT, by combining a commercial microfluidic device with nanopore sequencing to profile chromatin accessibility and histone modifications in individual cells. This addresses the throughput and scalability limitations of prior long-read single-cell approaches, enabling high-throughput profiling of multidimensional regulatory elements within single cells.

Overlapping yet distinct spatiomolecular profiles across mood disorders and biological sex in the human prefrontal cortex.

This study used spatial transcriptomics to profile the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of individuals with major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and neurotypical controls, revealing both overlapping and distinct molecular programs associated with diagnosis and biological sex. The findings show that mood disorders share some spatiomolecular features while also exhibiting diagnosis- and sex-specific differences in gene expression across cortical regions.

Overcoming segmentation bottlenecks in brain tissue for spatial proteomic inference at population scale.

The authors present SPInfer, a workflow for spatial proteomic inference that addresses the challenge of accurate cell segmentation in morphologically complex human brain tissue. Using 5,832 manually annotated cell bodies from 120 immunofluorescence images of the prefrontal cortex, they benchmark eight segmentation methods and show how domain adaptation affects downstream discovery at population scale. This work provides a practical solution for large-cohort spatial proteomics studies where segmentation quality is critical.

spaTransfer: transfer learning for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data using non-negative matrix factorization.

spaTransfer is a new computational method that uses non-negative matrix factorization to transfer cell type and spatial domain annotations from a reference single-cell or spatial transcriptomics atlas to new target samples. It is designed to handle references and targets that differ in resolution or were measured on different experimental platforms, addressing a key challenge in leveraging large-scale atlases.

Denoising single-cell ATAC-seq data with Shannon entropy.

The authors introduce a Shannon entropy-based method for filtering low-quality and empty droplets in single-cell ATAC-seq data. By using entropy as a measure of signal complexity rather than relying on read depth or predefined genomic features, the approach aims to better distinguish genuine nuclei from noisy droplets that can distort downstream analyses and mask rare cell populations.

CellWHISPER disentangles direct cell-cell communication from structural proximity.

CellWHISPER is a new computational framework for inferring direct, contact-dependent cell-cell communication (gap junctions and ligand-receptor signaling) from spatial transcriptomics data. It addresses a key problem in existing tools—high false-positive rates caused by confounding from cell-type-specific expression and spatial organization—by using a statistical procedure that controls for these effects and provides closed-form significance scores, enabling analysis of large datasets.

Spatial proximity to AD pathology defines cell-type and genotype-specific characteristics in human AD hippocampus.

This study developed a spatial transcriptomics pipeline combining MERFISH with concurrent annotation of amyloid-β plaques and AT8 phosphorylated tau in human control and Alzheimer's disease hippocampus. They identified cell-type-specific expression signatures in glia and neurons based on proximity to Aβ plaques, ptau-enriched neurons, or both pathologies together, and used these spatially defined signatures to infer pathology-associated states in large snRNA-seq datasets. The work links spatial proximity to AD pathology with cell-type and genotype-specific transcriptional responses.

Thermodynamic Quality Control Reshapes Spatially Resolved Metabolic Flux Predictions in Prostate Cancer.

The authors integrated spatial transcriptomics from twelve annotated regions of a prostate tumor with the Human-GEM metabolic model using an E-Flux framework, adding nutrient constraints and explicit thermodynamic cycle certification. They show that removing thermodynamically infeasible cycles (TICs) via loopless flux variability analysis substantially reshapes spatially resolved metabolic flux predictions across normal, inflamed, and Gleason 3+3/3+4 regions. The work demonstrates that thermodynamic quality control is essential for reliable spatial flux inference in cancer metabolism.

X-SPEAR: An Extensible Framework for Spatial Panel Evaluation and Refinement.

X-SPEAR is a framework for designing and evaluating targeted spatial transcriptomics gene panels (e.g., 10x Xenium), addressing the problem that genes detected in scRNA-seq references are often detected in fewer cells in the spatial assay, with gene-specific dropout. Its DART marker-selection method learns short Boolean gene rules and retains multiple gene-disjoint rules per cell type to improve rare-cell typing robustness.

Survival-associated cellular communication networks in human solid cancers.

PIANO enables generative modeling of gene expression and scales multi-omics integration to 100 million cells.

PIANO is a deep learning framework that uses a generative model of gene expression to integrate single-cell multi-omics data. It addresses three key challenges: correcting strong batch effects, scaling to millions of cells (demonstrated up to 100 million), and modeling how covariates influence expression. This enables more accurate and scalable integration of large transcriptomic atlases.

Sphinx: An R package for adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis in spatial omics.

Sphinx is an R package designed specifically for spatial proteomics data, offering a complete workflow from preprocessing and cell annotation to adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis. It introduces an adaptive parameter selection framework guided by spatial statistical metrics and includes computational optimizations for large-scale datasets, addressing the gap left by tools optimized primarily for spatial transcriptomics.

SigBridgeR: An R Toolkit for Standardized Identification and Benchmarking of Phenotype-Associated Cell Subpopulations in Single-Cell Transcriptomics.

SigBridgeR is an R toolkit that standardizes the identification and benchmarking of phenotype-associated cell subpopulations by integrating bulk transcriptomic data with single-cell RNA-seq data. It addresses the current fragmentation in the field—where different algorithms, parameters, and output formats make fair comparison and reproducibility difficult—by providing a unified framework for running and evaluating multiple methods. This enables researchers to more reliably determine which approach best links cell subpopulations to clinical phenotypes.

Disagreement-informed arbitration for gene regulatory network inference: A score-level meta-classifier and a diagnostic typology of inter-method conflict.

The authors propose a per-edge arbitration approach for gene regulatory network inference, training a gradient-boosted meta-classifier on the raw scores from ten different inference methods so that method weighting varies by edge rather than being fixed globally. They also introduce a diagnostic typology to characterize why methods disagree. Evaluated across six single-cell perturbation screens, this score-level arbitration aims to resolve inter-method conflicts more principledly than picking one method or simple averaging.

Integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analysis reveals an epithelial cell-derived prognostic and immunotherapeutic signature with ADAM12 as a key functional regulator in non-small cell lung cancer.

A categorization of spatial transcriptomics methods for cell-cell communication analysis.

This review categorizes 33 recent computational methods for inferring cell-cell communication from spatial transcriptomics data into three groups: cell-type or single-cell resolution network inference, microenvironment-driven transcriptional variability modeling, and regulatory modulation. It highlights how spatial context enables more biologically grounded communication inference than scRNA-seq alone and provides guidance for selecting methods based on the biological question.

A contextual activity score (CAS) for inferring ADAR-associated transcriptional activity across RNA-seq, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomics.

The authors introduce a Contextual Activity Score (CAS) that infers ADAR-associated RNA editing activity directly from gene expression data, bypassing the need for raw sequencing reads required by the standard Alu Editing Index. This makes it applicable to single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, where read-level editing quantification is impractical. The framework thus extends ADAR activity inference to a much broader range of transcriptomic technologies.

Residual disease as a therapy-remodeled ecosystem: spatial niches, tumor persistence, and relapse in solid tumors.

It links treatment-induced tissue changes—cell death, inflammation, repair, stromal activation, vascular injury, and metabolic stress—to the spatial niches where residual cells persist and to the timing of relapse-directed interventions, while cautioning that co-localization alone does not prove a protective niche.

Frontiers in immunology 2026--01 Low

Immune-chondrocyte ligand-receptor axes in osteoarthritis: microenvironmental control of inflammation, matrix remodeling, and chondrocyte fate.

This narrative review synthesizes evidence that osteoarthritis is a whole-joint disease driven by chronic low-grade inflammation, in which ligand-receptor communication between immune cells and chondrocytes translates microenvironmental cues into disease-relevant chondrocyte phenotypes. It catalogs major immune-derived or inflammation-amplified axes—such as IL-1β–IL-1R and TNF-α–TNFR—that regulate inflammation, matrix remodeling, and chondrocyte fate. The review frames these immune-chondrocyte interactions as central to OA progression rather than cartilage wear alone.
